title: About
description: What Nera is, its philosophy, and how to get involved.
content: About Nera Nera is an open-source static site generator with a deliberately small surface area. The whole pipeline — load, render, apply plugins, write — fits in a handful of files you can read in one sitting. Philosophy Transparent over magic. No hidden conventions; a page renders because its frontmatter says so. Composable over monolithic. Features live in small @nera-static/plugin-* packages you opt into. Yours to own. Templates publish into your project so you can style and edit them directly. Get involved Nera and its plugins are developed in the open on GitHub. Issues, ideas and pull requests are welcome — see the plugin catalog on the Plugins page. This site This website is itself built with Nera, using plugin-navigation, plugin-tags, plugin-search, plugin-page-pagination and plugin-canonical-links — plus one small local plugin for the tutorials list. Its source is on GitHub.

title: CLI reference
description: The nera CLI — scaffold, build, preview, update, validate and check a site.
content: CLI reference The nera CLI (@nera-static/nera) One command scaffolds, builds, previews, updates and validates a site. Scaffold a new one with: npx @nera-static/nera new <project-name> nera new . scaffolds into the current, empty folder instead, and --theme <name> starts the site from a theme. --starter <name> starts it from a ready-to-edit starter kit instead (blank, blog, business or portfolio; not together with --theme), and --name "<site name>" and --lang <code> set name and lang in config/app.yaml: npx @nera-static/nera new my-blog --starter blog --name "My Blog" --lang de --no-install skips the npm install at the end; run it yourself later. On a terminal, without --starter or --yes, nera new asks what you are building, the site name and the language; with --yes, or without a terminal, it never asks. Starter kits below has the details. A scaffolded site depends on @nera-static/nera, so run these from inside it with npx, e.g. npx nera validate. The scaffold also wires build, dev and serve to npm scripts, e.g. npm run dev: Command What it does nera build Build pages/ → public/; with --check, check the result too nera dev Build + live-reload preview on :3000 nera serve Serve public/ without rebuilding nera update Update the site's Nera packages (npm update) and raise their ^ ranges in package.json to the installed versions, then create or refresh AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md nera validate Check layouts, includes and YAML before publishing nera check Check the built public/ for accessibility, privacy and legal-notice problems Starter kits A starter kit is a whole ready-to-edit site: sample pages, config, optional site-level theme/ overrides, assets and the theme and plugins it depends on. nera new --starter copies its pages/, config/, theme/, assets/, plugins/ and .neraignore over the base template, adds its dependencies to the site's package.json, applies --name and --lang, installs, and prints the ## First steps section of the starter's README (nothing, when it has none). After that the site owns the files: a starter has no update path, though the theme it depends on still updates through npm. --name "<site name>" and --lang <code> set name: and lang: in config/app.yaml, with or without a starter. A new language gets a copy of the current language's translations: entry, ready to translate, so no page shows a raw translation key. --starter takes: a starter name: blank, blog, business or portfolio, short for @nera-static/starter-blank and so on; a package name: @acme/starter-shop, or unscoped nera-starter-shop; a GitHub URL: https://github.com/owner/repo (optionally .git, #ref), or github:owner/repo#ref; a local path: ./my-starter, ../my-starter or an absolute path. Packages and GitHub repositories are downloaded with npm pack --ignore-scripts, so no script of the starter runs. A starter is a package whose package.json has a nera.starter field ({ "label": "…", "description": "…" }); anything else is refused before anything is written. A starter that sets theme: in its config/app.yaml leaves out the scaffold's starter templates, as --theme does. Run nera new my-site on a terminal and it asks instead: What are you building? 1) Empty — the base template, no starter 2) … Choose 1–2 [1]: Site name [My Nera Site]: Language [en]: The list comes from the npm registry (packages with the keyword nera-starter, official @nera-static/ ones first), or from a short list bundled with the CLI when the registry cannot be reached. Enter accepts the default. Every question has a flag (--starter, --name, --lang); with --yes, or without a terminal (scripts, CI, AI agents), nothing is asked and nera new scaffolds the base template. The official starters: Starter What you get blank One accessible layout, no theme blog A blog on @nera-static/theme-blog with tags, an archive, an Atom feed and a sitemap business A small-business site on @nera-static/theme-business with services, opening hours and a contact form portfolio A designer's portfolio on @nera-static/theme-business with projects in image galleries, an about page and a contact form Checking the built site nera validate reads your sources. nera check reads what the build produced — the page a visitor gets, with its layout, navigation, footer, scripts, stylesheets and fonts — and looks for problems a parser can find there: nera build --check # build, then check — the one command for CI nera check # check an existing public/ without rebuilding Run nera build first; without public/, nera check stops with "run nera build first". A problem in a template is reported once, with the number of pages it appears on. Every finding is a warning by default, so the command exits 0. It exits 1 only when a rule you promoted to error fires — that is how you make it a CI gate. These are hints, not legal advice. A clean run is not proof of compliance: automated checks find only part of the accessibility problems (about a third of WCAG failures). Colour contrast, visible focus and whether a law applies to your site are not checked. Every report ends with that reminder. rule default basis a11y-html-lang warning WCAG 3.1.1 a11y-title warning WCAG 2.4.2 a11y-h1 warning WCAG 1.3.1 a11y-heading-skip warning WCAG 1.3.1 a11y-img-alt warning WCAG 1.1.1 a11y-form-label warning WCAG 1.3.1, 4.1.2 a11y-link-name warning WCAG 2.4.4, 4.1.2 a11y-main warning WCAG 1.3.1 a11y-skip-link warning WCAG 2.4.1 a11y-nav-name warning WCAG 1.3.1 a11y-duplicate-id warning WCAG 4.1.2 a11y-viewport-zoom warning WCAG 1.4.4 a11y-link-lang off (opt-in) WCAG 3.1.2 a11y-target-blank off (opt-in) WCAG 3.2.5 (AAA) a11y-reduced-motion off (opt-in) WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) privacy-third-party warning Art. 6 DSGVO privacy-consent-leak warning § 25 TDDDG privacy-insecure warning Art. 32 DSGVO privacy-storage off (opt-in) § 25 TDDDG legal-imprint-link warning § 5 DDG legal-privacy-link warning Art. 13 DSGVO legal-outdated-law warning DDG, TDDDG, MStV Configure the checks in config/validate.yaml (optional — without it the defaults above apply): rules: a11y-img-alt: error # promote: the check fails a11y-target-blank: warning # enable an opt-in rule a11y-skip-link: off # disable legal: imprint: # per language, the page every page links to de: /de/impressum.html en: /en/imprint.html privacy: de: /de/datenschutz.html en: /en/privacy.html privacy: allowed_hosts: # third-party hosts you have accounted for - cdn.example.org To silence a rule on one page, list it in the page's frontmatter as validate_ignore: [a11y-h1]. To silence a rule on whole files or folders, list them under ignore. This works for nera validate too — for example for layout-missing on content fragments that another page pulls in, or on drafts, which have no layout on purpose: ignore: layout-missing: - pages/*/references # a folder covers everything below it - pages/de/blog/drafts # * stands for one folder name Paths are relative to the site root. Requires @nera-static/validate 1.3.0, which npm update brings into an existing site. Your own host. To tell your resources from third-party ones, privacy-third-party reads origin from config/app.yaml, else app_origin from config/canonical-links.yaml (with and without www.). With neither set, only relative URLs count as your own. Consent-gated resources. A script or embed in the markup of @nera-static/plugin-consent (type="text/plain" with data-src, or data-consent-src instead of src) loads nothing on page view, so privacy-third-party does not report it. An element marked data-consent that still loads is what privacy-consent-leak reports. The tutorial Add a consent banner — or none shows both. Imprint and privacy links in German and English only. Without legal config, the links are found by their text — Impressum, Imprint, Legal notice, Datenschutz, Privacy, Data protection — and only on German and English pages. For any other language, name the pages under legal.imprint.<lang> and legal.privacy.<lang>. The full rule descriptions are in the @nera-static/validate README. Instructions for AI assistants Every scaffolded site carries an AGENTS.md — the file Codex, Cursor, Copilot and other assistants read first — and a CLAUDE.md holding the single line @AGENTS.md, so Claude Code loads the same text. AGENTS.md ends with a Notes for this site section for your own instructions, below the marker line <!-- nera:site-notes … -->. Keep that line in place: the part above it is Nera's, the part below it is yours. From @nera-static/nera 1.7.0 on, nera update keeps both files current, with no extra flag. After updating the packages (and after nera update --migrate) it: creates AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md when they are missing, so an older site gets them too; replaces only the part of AGENTS.md above the marker line with the text from the installed @nera-static/nera; the marker line and your notes below it stay exactly as they are; leaves an AGENTS.md without the marker line alone and prints a hint — copy the marker line from the template directly above your own notes to opt in; never touches an existing CLAUDE.md. A file is written only when its content changes, so running nera update again changes nothing. Migrating an older (cloned) site Sites created before the CLI were git clones that vendored the engine under src/. Inside such a site, run nera update --migrate — it adds the @nera-static/nera dependency, rewrites the scripts, removes the vendored src/ engine, and installs, leaving your pages/, config/ and theme/ untouched. Plugin publish commands Each template-shipping plugin exposes a bin to copy its Pug into theme/views/vendor/, e.g.: npx nera-navigation npx nera-tags npx nera-search --force # overwrite existing published templates

title: Core concepts
description: The render pipeline, the app and meta objects, layouts and translations.
content: Core concepts The four-stage pipeline Every build runs the same fixed pipeline: load app data → render pages → apply plugins → write output. Understanding these four stages explains almost everything about how Nera behaves. app vs meta Two data objects reach your templates: app — global values from config/app.yaml, available on every page. meta — per-page values: your frontmatter, plus derived keys like meta.href, meta.dirname, meta.filename and meta.createdAt. Plugins add to both — for example, plugin-navigation sets app.nav, and plugin-tags sets meta.tagLinks. Layouts Layouts are Pug files under theme/views/. A page's layout frontmatter picks one: --- layout: pages/docs.pug title: My page --- The path is relative to theme/views/, so pages/docs.pug is theme/views/pages/docs.pug. If config/app.yaml sets theme: (a package such as @nera-static/theme-example, or a local folder), the layouts come from that theme, and a file in your own theme/views/ or theme/assets/ replaces the theme's file at the same path — override one template without copying the rest. npx @nera-static/nera new my-site --theme example starts a site that way. Translations config/app.yaml holds a translations map. In a layout, t('key') resolves app.translations[meta.lang || app.lang][key], falling back to the key itself — so missing translations are visible, not silent.

title: Deployment
description: Building the site and hosting the public/ folder.
content: Deployment Nera outputs a plain public/ folder — deploy it anywhere that serves static files. Build npm run build Host it Netlify / Vercel — build command npm run build, publish directory public. GitHub Pages — build in GitHub Actions and deploy public/ with actions/upload-pages-artifact and actions/deploy-pages, as this site does. Any static host / CDN — upload the contents of public/. Cache busting Browsers cache stylesheets, scripts and fonts, so after a deploy visitors may keep seeing the old CSS or JS until they force a reload. Turn on content hashing in config/app.yaml (requires @nera-static/core 4.11 or newer): asset_hashing: true On every build Nera appends ?v=<hash> to each local asset URL — stylesheets, scripts, images, srcset, the search index and url(…) references inside CSS such as fonts. The hash comes from the file's content, so a URL changes exactly when its file does and stays cacheable otherwise. Your templates keep plain paths like /css/main.css; never add ?v= by hand. Page links, external URLs and URLs that already have a query string are left alone, and it works together with base_path. Without the key the build output is unchanged. Before you launch Set origin in config/app.yaml to your real domain so canonical URLs are correct (see Canonical links for SEO). Add an .neraignore at the project root to keep source-only assets out of the build. public/ is deleted and rebuilt on every render — never edit it by hand, and never commit it as source.

title: Getting started
description: Scaffold a new Nera site with the nera CLI and build it.
content: Getting started Requirements Node.js 22.12 or newer npm 10.9 or newer (bundled with Node.js 22.12) Scaffold a site nera new scaffolds a new site whose one Nera dependency is @nera-static/nera, which brings the @nera-static/core engine — no clone, no vendored source: npx @nera-static/nera new my-site cd my-site npm run dev npm run dev renders the site and starts a live-reloading preview on http://localhost:3000. Already in the folder the site should live in? npx @nera-static/nera new . scaffolds into the current, empty folder. Rather start from a ready-to-edit site? --starter <name> scaffolds from a starter kit such as blog or business; see Starter kits. Build for production npm run build This deletes and regenerates public/. Deploy that folder to any static host. Update later npx nera update nera update bumps the site's Nera packages with npm update and refreshes Nera's part of AGENTS.md, leaving your pages/, config/ and theme/ untouched. From @nera-static/nera 1.15.0 on, it also raises their ^ ranges in package.json (and package-lock.json) to the versions it installed, so ^1.0.0 becomes, say, ^1.15.0; it never crosses a major version. How an AI assistant uses AGENTS.md is explained in Using Nera with AI.

title: Introduction
description: What Nera is, how it works, and where to go next.
content: Documentation Nera is a lightweight static site generator built on a simple idea: Markdown in, HTML out, with plugins for everything else. This guide takes you from an empty folder to a deployed site. The shape of a Nera project my-site/ ├── config/ # app.yaml + one <plugin>.yaml per plugin ├── pages/ # your Markdown content ├── theme/ │ ├── views/ # Pug layouts and page templates (vendor/ holds plugin templates) │ └── assets/ # CSS, JS, images, fonts — copied verbatim to public/ ├── src/plugins/ # optional local plugins, one folder each ├── public/ # generated output (never edit by hand) ├── AGENTS.md # instructions for AI assistants (CLAUDE.md points to it) └── package.json # one Nera dependency: @nera-static/nera nera new creates everything here except src/plugins/ and public/. Local plugins can live in another folder, set with folders.plugins in config/app.yaml. Sites from before the theme system keep views/ and assets/ at the project root; Nera still builds them, with a deprecation warning, until you move both folders under theme/. How a page becomes HTML Load config/app.yaml into the app object and list pages/. Render each Markdown file, extracting frontmatter into meta. Apply plugins, which enrich app and meta. Write public/, running each page through its layout. A page is only rendered if its frontmatter sets a layout. Pages without one are silently skipped — this is the single most common "why is my page missing?" npx nera validate lists them (layout-missing). Continue to Getting started to scaffold your first site. Working with an AI assistant? Read Using Nera with AI.

title: Plugins
description: Installing plugins, the hook contract, config resolution, and templates.
content: Plugins Installing npm install @nera-static/plugin-navigation Any dependency whose name starts with @nera-static/plugin- is discovered and applied automatically — no registration step. (@nera-static/plugin-utils is a helper library, not a plugin, and is skipped.) A plugin for one site only needs no package: put it in src/plugins/<name>/index.js, or set another folder with folders.plugins in config/app.yaml. See Write your own local plugin. The hook contract A plugin is an ESM module exporting up to three hooks, getAppData, getMetaData and getAssets (below): export function getAppData({ app, pagesData }) { return { ...app, myKey: 'value' } // must return a plain object } export function getMetaData({ app, pagesData }) { return pagesData // must return an array } getAppData runs first; getMetaData sees the app it returned. Core awaits every hook (since core 4.3.0; older versions silently replaced app with a Promise), but synchronous stays the safe default — it is what the published plugins do. A plugin that produces files (generated images, for example) also exports getAssets (core ≥ 4.13.0). It runs after every plugin's getAppData and getMetaData, sees the final app and pagesData, and returns what to copy into public/: export function getAssets({ app, pagesData }) { return [{ from: '/abs/path/to/files', to: '_img' }] } from is an absolute file or folder, to a path inside public/. Core copies these after the theme's assets and before your own, so your theme/assets/ still wins on a name clash. Invalid entries are skipped with a warning. Config lives in your project Every plugin reads config/<name>.yaml from your site, not from the package. The YAML shipped inside the package is documentation; copy it into your config/ and edit. Missing keys fall back to sensible defaults. Ordering config/plugin-order.yaml controls execution order: names under start: run first, then everything else alphabetically, then names under end:. Search runs last so it indexes the final page data. Templates Plugins that ship views expose a publish command: npx nera-navigation # copies templates into theme/views/vendor/plugin-navigation/ Then include them from your layouts. Publishing skips if the folder already exists — delete it (or pass --force) to pull in template updates.

title: Using Nera with AI
description: Work on a Nera site with an AI assistant — AGENTS.md, docs for AI, the check loop and example prompts.
content: Using Nera with AI AI assistants know Eleventy, Hugo and Astro well, and Nera hardly at all. Left alone, they guess — and guess wrong: pretty URLs, a missing layout, edits in public/. Nera gives them the facts in two ways: an instruction file in every site, and its docs as plain Markdown. What every site ships A site created with npx @nera-static/nera new (from @nera-static/nera 1.6.0 on) contains two files for AI assistants: AGENTS.md — the instruction file read by Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and other assistants. It says what Nera is (and that it is not Eleventy, Hugo, Astro or Jekyll), maps the folders, lists the commands, names the usual traps — a page needs layout, URLs end in .html, public/ is wiped on every build — and says to look in the plugin catalog before writing a feature. From 1.8.0 on it also links Nera's docs for AI (see below). CLAUDE.md — one line, @AGENTS.md, so Claude Code loads the same text. AGENTS.md ends with a Notes for this site section below the marker line <!-- nera:site-notes … -->. That part is yours: write down the audience, the tone, the languages, pages that must not change and where the site is hosted. The part above the marker is Nera's. An existing site? From @nera-static/nera 1.7.0 on, npx nera update creates AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md when they are missing and refreshes only Nera's part of AGENTS.md, so your notes stay. The details are in the CLI reference, under "Instructions for AI assistants". The Nera skill From @nera-static/nera 1.10.0 on, every new site also contains the Nera skill, an Agent Skill: a SKILL.md with the workflow and the checks to run, plus short recipes for a business site, a blog, a portfolio, a contact form, search, images, a second language and a custom domain. Assistants that support skills load it when a task is about Nera. It sits in two folders: .agents/skills/nera/ — read by Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Gemini CLI; .claude/skills/nera/ — read by Claude Code. Both folders are Nera's: npx nera update adds them to an existing site and keeps them in step with the installed version, so commit them but do not edit them. Write your own notes in AGENTS.md instead. claude.ai and Claude Desktop install skills by upload. Download nera-skill.zip — the same skill a new site gets — and upload it in the skills section of the settings. Per assistant Open the site's folder in the assistant — the folder with package.json and AGENTS.md — so it finds the instructions. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, which pulls in AGENTS.md. OpenAI Codex reads AGENTS.md. Cursor, GitHub Copilot and other coding assistants that support the AGENTS.md convention read it too. Chat assistants without access to your files (claude.ai, ChatGPT and the like) never see AGENTS.md. Give them Nera's docs in the prompt instead — see the next section. Docs for AI nera.js.org publishes its docs for assistants, in English: https://nera.js.org/llms.txt — an index of the docs, following the llms.txt convention; https://nera.js.org/llms-full.txt — all English docs and tutorials in one Markdown file; a raw Markdown file beside every English docs and tutorials page, e.g. /docs/cli.md next to /docs/cli.html. Paste one of these URLs into a chat assistant's prompt, or attach the file. The docs are English only on purpose: models read them well and answer in your language. The workflow Ask for one change at a time. Let the assistant edit the files. It runs npx nera validate, then npx nera build --check, and fixes what they report. AGENTS.md tells it to; say so in the prompt if it does not. With --json (from 1.9.0 on) both print their findings for machines. Preview with npm run dev on http://localhost:3000. Review the diff (git diff) before you publish. Example prompts Create a new site — there is no AGENTS.md yet, so name the command and the docs: Create a new Nera site in the folder "bakery" with npx @nera-static/nera new bakery, then read its AGENTS.md before changing anything. Nera's docs are at https://nera.js.org/llms.txt. Add a page: Add an "About us" page at pages/about.md with the same layout as pages/index.md, and link it from the menu (add @nera-static/plugin-navigation if the site has no menu yet). Then run npx nera validate and npx nera build --check and fix what they report. Add a contact form with the plugin: Add a contact form to the contact page with @nera-static/plugin-contact-form. Install it, copy its template with its command, include it in the page template and set my address in config/contact-form.yaml. Do not write a form by hand. Add a second language: Add German as a second language. Put the German pages under pages/de/, set lang: de in their frontmatter, move the interface text into translations in config/app.yaml and use t('key') in the templates. Fix what nera validate reports: Run npx nera validate and fix every error and warning it reports. Explain each fix in one line. Then run npx nera build --check. In a chat assistant without file access: Read https://nera.js.org/llms-full.txt — the docs of the Nera static site generator. Then explain how I add a blog section with tags to my Nera site, with the files I need to create and their content. What's planned Planned, not available yet: nera publish — getting a site online from the CLI; an MCP server for Nera: a local one for Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor, and a hosted connector for claude.ai and ChatGPT that works on your GitHub repository.

title: Writing content
description: Markdown files, frontmatter, and the derived meta values.
content: Writing content A content file Each page is a Markdown file under pages/ with a YAML frontmatter block: --- layout: pages/default.pug title: About description: What this page is about. --- # About Your content goes here. Who writes the title title is data, not output. Whether it reaches the page is up to the layout, so check before repeating it in the body: If the layout renders meta.title itself, leave the heading out of the Markdown — writing # About as well puts the title on the page twice. If it doesn't, the body's own # heading is the page's only title, as in the example above. On this site pages/default.pug and pages/docs.pug render no title, so those pages open with a heading. The tutorial, tutorials-index, plugins and tag-overview layouts do render it, so their Markdown starts straight into the prose. Frontmatter is data Everything in frontmatter lands on meta. Use it for titles, descriptions, tags, ordering — anything a layout or plugin should read. YAML types are preserved: numbers stay numbers, booleans stay booleans. Guard on meta.x != null, not if (meta.x), so a legitimate 0 or false survives. Derived meta values Nera adds these automatically: Key Meaning meta.href URL path of the generated HTML file meta.dirname Directory the page lives in meta.filename Source filename meta.createdAt createdAt or date from the frontmatter, else the file's creation time Set createdAt (or date) in the frontmatter of anything sorted by date, such as posts. A fresh checkout in CI gives every file the same creation time, so without it the order is lost on the build server. Folders become URLs pages/docs/getting-started.md → /docs/getting-started.html. Nesting folders nests URLs — no routing config required.

title: Add client-side search
description: Wire up plugin-search to generate an index and a working search box.
content: @nera-static/plugin-search builds a JSON index at render time and ships a small client script — no server required. 1. Install npm install @nera-static/plugin-search 2. Publish the template npx nera-search This copies the search box into theme/views/vendor/plugin-search/ and the client into theme/assets/js/search.js. Both copies are yours from then on. Running npx nera-search again skips the template if the vendor/plugin-search/ folder exists and the client if search.js exists, so it never discards your edits — and a template change in a new release never reaches your site on its own. To refresh after an upgrade, run npx nera-search --force, but only if you never edited the copies: it overwrites both. If you did, diff them against the package and merge the changes by hand (the plugin README's Template Publishing section explains how). 3. Configure config/search.yaml controls which fields are indexed. The file is optional; these are the defaults: fields: - title - excerpt - content - href strip_html: true output_filename: search-index.json fields replaces the default list rather than extending it, so keep content (the page body) and href (the result link). Any other frontmatter key works if your pages define it — the starter page nera new scaffolds has a description but no excerpt, so add description if you want it indexed; a field a page lacks is simply left off its entry. To keep part of a page out of the index, mark it with data-search-ignore: the element and everything inside it is dropped from content. @nera-static/plugin-code-blocks (1.1.0 and later) marks its code-block bar this way, so file names and the Copy button stay out of your results. In Markdown, write the attribute on raw HTML: <aside data-search-ignore>Not part of the index.</aside> 4. Add a search page The search box is Pug, so it belongs in a view, not in the Markdown. Create theme/views/pages/search.pug on top of the layout nera new scaffolds: extends ../layouts/layout block content main article!= content include /vendor/plugin-search/search.pug The leading slash resolves the include from theme/views/. Then point a page at the view — a page without layout is neither rendered nor indexed: --- title: Search layout: pages/search.pug --- # Search Search across the documentation. That page brings its own # Search heading, so turn off the template's h1 in config/search.yaml, or nera build --check warns a11y-h1 about two of them: show_title: false If your page has no heading of its own, leave show_title out and the template's h1 is the page heading. The template's texts go through t(): search_title (the heading, default Search), search_placeholder (default Search...) and search_label, the input's accessible name (default Search). Translate them under translations in config/app.yaml, for example for German: translations: de: search_title: Suche search_placeholder: Suchen… search_label: Suche Finally, make sure search runs last in config/plugin-order.yaml so it indexes final page data, including pages other plugins generate: plugin-order: - end: - plugin-search 5. Per-language search (optional) By default every page lands in one index, so the search box on a German page also returns English and Spanish hits. Set group_by_lang to give each language an index of its own: group_by_lang: true Pages are grouped by meta.lang, and the language code goes before the extension of output_filename. The default language keeps the plain filename: /search-index.json # default language /search-index.de.json # German pages only /search-index.es.json # Spanish pages only Pages without a meta.lang fall into the default language — lang in config/app.yaml — so a single-language site is unaffected by any of this. Every page then carries meta.searchIndexPath, the index for its own language. The published search.pug passes it to the client as data-search-index and search.js fetches that URL, so your own markup needs no change. Watch one detail — app.searchIndexPath still exists, but with grouping on it points at the default language's index, so building the attribute from it would search English from a German page. app.searchIndexPaths has every language keyed by code, and each index entry carries its lang. Because search runs last (step 4), pages other plugins generate land in the right language too — the tag pages from plugin-tags among them. Render, and you have working search. This site's Search page is built from the same parts, with two differences: its Markdown has no heading, so it keeps the template's h1, translated with the three keys in English, German and Spanish; and it sets group_by_lang: true, so the box returns only pages in the language you are reading.

title: Build a blog with Nera
description: Scaffold a site, write posts, and list them newest-first on the home page with plugin-simple-page-list.
content: In this tutorial you'll scaffold a Nera site, write two posts, and turn the home page into a blog index that lists them newest-first. Every file is shown in full, so you can follow along step by step. 1. Scaffold the site npx @nera-static/nera new my-blog cd my-blog nera new creates the site and installs its dependencies. You'll touch three places: pages/ for your content (it starts with pages/index.md, plus pages/imprint.md and pages/privacy.md — placeholders to replace before you publish), theme/views/ for the Pug templates (layouts/layout.pug is the HTML shell, pages/default.pug renders a page into it), and config/ for settings. Want a finished blog to edit instead? The blog starter sets one up with a theme, sample posts, tags, an archive, a feed and a sitemap: npx @nera-static/nera new my-blog --starter blog Its files won't match the steps below: this tutorial builds a simpler blog by hand, to show how the pieces fit together. 2. Write posts Posts are Markdown files in pages/posts/. Create pages/posts/hello-world.md: --- layout: pages/default.pug title: Hello world description: My first post. createdAt: 2026-10-01 --- # Hello world Welcome to my new Nera blog. And a second one, pages/posts/second-post.md: --- layout: pages/default.pug title: My second post description: What I learned this week. createdAt: 2026-10-08 --- # My second post A week in, and the blog lists this post first. A page renders only if it names a layout. The title and description show up in the list, and createdAt is the post's date. Always set it: without it, Nera falls back to the file's creation time, which on a fresh checkout — on a CI build server, say — is the same for every file, so the order would be arbitrary. 3. List the posts on the home page @nera-static/plugin-simple-page-list collects the pages of a folder into a sorted list. Install it and publish its template: npm install @nera-static/plugin-simple-page-list npx nera-simple-page-list Nera picks up the plugin from your package.json on its own. The second command copies the template to theme/views/vendor/plugin-simple-page-list/simple-page-list.pug. Tell the plugin which folder to list and how to sort it. Create config/simple-page-list.yaml: page_path: /posts more_link_text: Read more sortBy: date sortOrder: descending page_path gives you one flat list in app.pageList, which is all a blog with one section needs. sortBy: date reads a post's date from the frontmatter and falls back to createdAt, so your posts sort by the dates you just set. Now a page template that renders the page's own content and the list below it. Create theme/views/pages/blog.pug: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main != content include /vendor/plugin-simple-page-list/simple-page-list The two contents are unrelated. block content fills the slot of that name in layouts/layout.pug. != content outputs the page's Markdown, which Nera has already rendered to HTML; != leaves it unescaped, so it arrives as markup. The leading slash makes the include path start at theme/views/, wherever the template sits. Finally, make the home page use it. Replace pages/index.md with: --- layout: pages/blog.pug title: My blog description: Notes and posts, newest first. --- # My blog Welcome! Here is everything I have written so far. This is the template you published — yours to edit: //- Handles both shapes `getAppData` can produce: //- flat — `app.pageList` is an array (config uses `page_path`) //- grouped — `app.pageList` is keyed by path (config uses `page_paths`) //- The flat branch emits exactly the markup this template has always emitted, //- so published copies keep rendering identically. mixin pageListItems(pages) each page in pages article.page-list__item header.page-list__header h3.page-list__item-title a.page-list__link(href=page.href) #{page.title} if page.description p.page-list__description #{page.description} footer.page-list__footer a.page-list__more-link(href=page.href) #{page.moreLinkText} - var pageList = app.pageList var isFlat = Array.isArray(pageList) var groups = [] if (isFlat) { groups = pageList.length ? [{ key: null, pages: pageList }] : [] } else if (pageList && typeof pageList === 'object') { groups = Object.keys(pageList) .filter(function (key) { return Array.isArray(pageList[key]) && pageList[key].length > 0 }) .map(function (key) { return { key: key, pages: pageList[key] } }) } if groups.length > 0 section.page-list h2.page-list__title Recent Pages if isFlat +pageListItems(groups[0].pages) else each group in groups div.page-list__group h3.page-list__group-title #{group.key} +pageListItems(group.pages) Each post becomes an article with its title, description and a "Read more" link, under the heading "Recent Pages". To change the heading or the markup, edit this file — it is your copy now. Running npx nera-simple-page-list again skips the folder because it already exists; npx nera-simple-page-list --force overwrites it with the shipped version and discards your edits. Prefer to write the list yourself? See Write your own local plugin. 4. Grow it Tags: give posts tags: and get a page per tag with Tag your content. Previous/next links: link each post to its neighbours in pages/posts/ with Add prev/next links between pages. Sitemap: set your site's origin as in Add canonical links for SEO, then add @nera-static/plugin-sitemap from the plugin catalog. Images and code: @nera-static/plugin-images (responsive images) and @nera-static/plugin-code-blocks (syntax highlighting) are in the plugin catalog too. 5. Preview and build npm run dev Open http://localhost:3000: the home page lists "My second post" above "Hello world", and each title links to its post. The preview rebuilds when you save a file. When you're ready to publish, build the site once: npm run build The finished blog is in public/ — upload that folder to any static host.

title: Add canonical links for SEO
description: Use plugin-canonical-links to emit correct canonical and alternate-language link tags, including on subdirectory sites and generated pages.
content: Search engines want a single canonical URL per page, and on a multilingual site they want to know which pages are translations of each other. @nera-static/plugin-canonical-links emits the <link rel="canonical"> tag on every page and hreflang alternate tags between translations. Get these wrong and nothing breaks visibly — the page renders fine, and the mistake only shows up in a search console weeks later. So check the output, as this tutorial does at every step. 1. Install and publish the template npm install @nera-static/plugin-canonical-links npx nera-canonical-links The second command copies index.pug and its partials/ to theme/views/vendor/plugin-canonical-links/. It skips if that folder already exists, so your edits are safe; npx nera-canonical-links --force overwrites them with the shipped templates after an upgrade. 2. Set your origin Canonical URLs are absolute, so the plugin needs your site's origin. Set it once in config/app.yaml: origin: https://example.com That is all the configuration a single-language site needs — the plugin's own config file is optional. If you do create config/canonical-links.yaml, its app_origin is used as a fallback when app.yaml has no origin; when both are set, origin in app.yaml wins. A trailing slash is stripped either way. With no origin at all, the plugin emits no canonical or alternate links and prints one warning during the build: ⚠️ plugin-canonical-links: no origin configured, so no canonical links were generated. Set `origin` in config/app.yaml, or `app_origin` in config/canonical-links.yaml. If your site is served from a subdirectory, base_path in config/app.yaml is part of the URL too. Canonical and alternate URLs are built as origin + base path page path: origin: https://example.com base_path: /docs/ <link href="https://example.com/docs/getting-started.html" rel="canonical" /> Without base_path the output is unchanged. Versions before 2.2.3 left the base path out and pointed search engines at a URL that does not exist. 3. Emit the tags The plugin sets meta.canonicalLink on every page. Include the published template in your layout's <head>: head include /vendor/plugin-canonical-links/index The leading slash makes the path root-absolute: it resolves against theme/views/, wherever the including file sits. The relative form include ../vendor/plugin-canonical-links/index does the same, but only from a layout in theme/views/layouts/ — use it on Nera core 4.1–4.2, where the root-absolute form is not available yet. A bare include vendor/… (no slash, no ../) looks in theme/views/layouts/vendor/ and fails the build. Build and view the source of pages/getting-started.md — you'll see: <link href="https://example.com/getting-started.html" rel="canonical" /> 4. Link translations with hreflang Alternate-language links need three things. First, list your languages in config/canonical-links.yaml: page_identifier: slug available_languages: - en - de page_identifier names the frontmatter key that marks two pages as translations of each other; slug is the default, so you can leave the line out. Second, every page sets its lang. Third, translations share an identical slug: --- title: Getting started slug: getting-started lang: en --- --- title: Erste Schritte slug: getting-started lang: de --- With the English page at pages/getting-started.md and the German one at pages/de/getting-started.md, the build gives the English page: <link href="https://example.com/getting-started.html" rel="canonical" /> <link href="https://example.com/de/getting-started.html" hreflang="de" rel="alternate" /> and the German page: <link href="https://example.com/de/getting-started.html" rel="canonical" /> <link href="https://example.com/getting-started.html" hreflang="en" rel="alternate" /> Each page points at its translations, not at itself. All of this fails silently: Without available_languages you get canonical links only, and meta.alternateLinks is an empty array. A page without lang gets its canonical link but no alternates. A page without a slug is never matched to anything. If you write your own template instead of the published one, read meta.alternateLinks — a list of { href, hreflang, rel } — and guard for both keys being absent when no origin is set. 5. Cover pages from other plugins Some plugins create pages while they run — @nera-static/plugin-tags builds its tag overview pages that way (see Tag your content). Plugins run in alphabetical order, and plugin-canonical-links comes before plugin-tags, so those tag pages are built after it has finished and get no canonical link. Move it to the end in config/plugin-order.yaml (Nera core 4.2.0 or newer): plugin-order: - end: - plugin-canonical-links Now every tag page carries one: <link href="https://example.com/tags/seo.html" rel="canonical" /> Generated pages have no slug, so they get a canonical link and no alternates. The sitemap plugin, @nera-static/plugin-sitemap, reads the same origin (origin in app.yaml, else app_origin) and the same base_path, so the URLs in your sitemap and your canonical links agree — on a base_path site from plugin-canonical-links 2.2.3 on. This site uses the plugin as well, set up as this tutorial describes: origin: https://nera.js.org in config/app.yaml, the root-absolute include in its layout, and plugin-canonical-links under end: in config/plugin-order.yaml. Its config/canonical-links.yaml lists only en and de as languages — Spanish is left out until a native-speaker review is done, so no page carries an hreflang="es" alternate yet. View the source of this page to see the result.

title: Add a consent banner — or none — with plugin-consent
description: Find out whether your site needs a consent banner at all, then gate a YouTube embed and an analytics script with plugin-consent so nothing loads before the visitor agrees.
content: A consent banner asks visitors to agree before something on the site that needs their consent runs: an analytics script, a YouTube video, a map. A site that loads none of that has nothing to ask. @nera-static/plugin-consent covers both cases: it shows a short info notice (or nothing) on a site without such services, and a banner with a settings dialog on a site with them, and it keeps every configured script and embed inert until the visitor agrees. Every command, config and output below was run in a fresh nera new site with plugin-consent 1.0.2 and @nera-static/validate 1.6.2. 1. Do you need a banner at all? Start with what your site loads from other hosts. Every font, video, map or script from a third-party server sends the visitor's IP address there, and much of it sets cookies. The first option is not a banner but not loading it from elsewhere: serve fonts from your own site (this site's IBM Plex lives in theme/assets/fonts/), serve a video file from your own host with <video>, or link to the video instead of embedding it, run the statistics tool yourself, or do without one. Self-hosting removes the third-party request. It does not by itself settle whether a tool that stores something on the visitor's device needs consent; that depends on what it stores and why. The background, in more depth: Do I need a cookie banner? If nothing is left that needs consent, you need no banner. You can still install the plugin: without a config/consent.yaml, or with one that lists no categories, it is in notice mode and renders a short notice: <section class="nera-consent nera-consent--notice" data-consent-notice="data-consent-notice" data-consent-revision="1" aria-labelledby="nera-consent-notice-text" hidden="hidden"> <p class="nera-consent__text" id="nera-consent-notice-text">This site uses only technically necessary cookies. <a class="nera-consent__link" href="/privacy.html">Privacy policy</a></p> <div class="nera-consent__actions"><button class="nera-consent__button" type="button" data-consent-dismiss="data-consent-dismiss">Got it</button></div> </section> The runtime shows it until the visitor clicks "Got it". If you do not want even that, set notice: false: privacy_url: /privacy.html notice: false app.consent.mode is then 'none', and the views render nothing at all. Once you add a category, notice: false no longer applies, and the build says so: ⚠️ plugin-consent: config/consent.yaml: ignoring notice: false, the site has categories and shows the banner 2. Install and wire the layout npm install @nera-static/plugin-consent npx nera-consent-config npx nera-consent npx nera-consent-config copies the documented config/consent.yaml, every example commented out, so the site starts in notice mode. npx nera-consent copies the five views (banner, settings, notice, head, embed). On a site scaffolded with nera new, they land in theme/views/vendor/plugin-consent/. Both commands skip a file or folder that already exists; --force overwrites it, and your edits with it. Plugins cannot touch your layout, so this is the one manual step. Add the stylesheet, the head view and the runtime inside <head>, a settings link in the footer, and the three other views at the end of <body>: <!DOCTYPE html> html(lang=app.lang) head meta(charset="UTF-8") meta(name="viewport", content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0") title #{ meta.title } | #{ app.name } link(rel='stylesheet' href='/_nera/consent.css') include /vendor/plugin-consent/head script(src='/_nera/consent.js' defer) body a.skip-link(href="#main") #{ t('skip_to_content') } block content footer a(href="/imprint.html") #{ t('imprint') } = ' · ' a(href="/privacy.html") #{ t('privacy') } = ' · ' a(href='/privacy.html' data-consent-open) Privacy settings include /vendor/plugin-consent/banner include /vendor/plugin-consent/settings include /vendor/plugin-consent/notice (The scaffold's other meta tags and its style block stay as they are; they are left out here.) consent.css and consent.js are copied to public/_nera/ on every build, in every mode. The runtime needs defer. banner, settings and notice each render only in their own mode, so include all three. Any element with data-consent-open opens the settings dialog, where the visitor can change or withdraw a choice at any time. On a link, the href is the fallback for a page without the dialog or without JavaScript. The plugin needs @nera-static/core 4.13.0 or later, which every current @nera-static/nera brings. 3. Gate a YouTube embed Paste the embed code into a page as usual: --- layout: pages/default.pug title: Our video description: A page with an embedded video --- # Our video <iframe src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/abc123" title="Our video" width="560" height="315" allowfullscreen></iframe> Then describe the service in config/consent.yaml, in one category: revision: 1 privacy_url: /privacy.html categories: - id: media services: - name: YouTube provider: Google Ireland Limited, Dublin purpose: Shows embedded videos. privacy_url: https://policies.google.com/privacy hosts: [youtube.com, youtube-nocookie.com] cookies: - name: VISITOR_INFO1_LIVE duration: 6 months purpose: Estimates the visitor's bandwidth. id: media is one of four ids with a built-in label and description in English and German (analytics, media, marketing, functional); any other id needs a label. name, provider and purpose are required; a service without them is dropped with a warning. hosts are bare host names. An <iframe> whose src host equals one of them or is a subdomain of it is gated: www.youtube-nocookie.com matches youtube-nocookie.com. cookies are listed in the settings dialog. The entry above is an example: list what the provider documents. With a category configured, the site is in banner mode. After nera build, the iframe in public/video.html has no src left; its URL moved to data-consent-src, and a placeholder follows it: <div class="nera-consent-embed" data-consent-embed data-consent="media"><iframe data-consent="media" data-consent-src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/abc123" title="Our video" width="560" height="315" allowfullscreen hidden></iframe> <div class="nera-consent-embed__placeholder"> <p class="nera-consent-embed__text">This content is provided by YouTube. Loading it connects to <strong>Google Ireland Limited, Dublin</strong>.</p><button class="nera-consent-embed__load" type="button" data-consent-load>Load YouTube</button><a class="nera-consent-embed__privacy" href="https://policies.google.com/privacy" rel="noopener">Privacy policy of the provider</a><button class="nera-consent-embed__settings" type="button" data-consent-open>Privacy settings</button> </div> </div> In a browser, the test page made no request to another host until a click. "Load YouTube" loaded this one embed and stored nothing; "Accept all" in the banner stored the choice and loaded every gated element. The banner itself puts Accept all, Reject all and Settings on the first layer, in that fixed order and one shared style: <section class="nera-consent" data-consent-banner="data-consent-banner" data-consent-revision="1" data-consent-categories="media" aria-labelledby="nera-consent-title" hidden="hidden"> <h2 class="nera-consent__title" id="nera-consent-title">Cookies and external content</h2> <p class="nera-consent__text">This site can load content and services from third parties. They only load if you agree. You can change your choice at any time in the settings. <a class="nera-consent__link" href="/privacy.html">Privacy policy</a></p> <div class="nera-consent__actions"><button class="nera-consent__button" type="button" data-consent-accept-all="data-consent-accept-all">Accept all</button><button class="nera-consent__button" type="button" data-consent-reject-all="data-consent-reject-all">Reject all</button><button class="nera-consent__button" type="button" data-consent-open="data-consent-open">Settings</button></div> </section> <embed>, <object>, <video> and <audio> from a configured host are gated the same way. Two places the build does not reach: An iframe written directly into a Pug view is not rewritten. Use the mixin from the published embed view there; it renders the same placeholder: include /vendor/plugin-consent/embed +consent-embed({ category: 'media', service: 'YouTube', src: 'https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/abc123', attributes: { title: 'Our video', width: 560, height: 315, allowfullscreen: true }, }) category and service must name a configured service, or the build fails rather than render a live iframe. A gated <video>, <audio> or <embed> written inline in a Markdown paragraph ends up inside a <p>, which the browser splits around the placeholder. Put its opening tag alone on a line, after a blank line. 4. Gate an analytics script A script you configure under a service's scripts is emitted by the head view, inert. Add a second category: revision: 2 privacy_url: /privacy.html categories: - id: media # … YouTube as above - id: analytics services: - name: Matomo provider: Example GmbH, Berlin purpose: Counts visits without profiles. cookies: - name: _pk_id duration: 13 months purpose: Recognises returning visitors. scripts: - inline: | var _paq = window._paq = window._paq || []; _paq.push(['trackPageView']); - src: https://matomo.example.com/matomo.js async: true Each script entry has exactly one of src and inline. In the built <head>, both are type="text/plain", which the browser does not run, and the URL sits in data-src: <link rel="stylesheet" href="/_nera/consent.css" /> <script type="text/plain" data-consent="analytics">var _paq = window._paq = window._paq || []; _paq.push(['trackPageView']); </script> <script type="text/plain" data-consent="analytics" data-src="https://matomo.example.com/matomo.js" async="async"></script> <script src="/_nera/consent.js" defer="defer"></script> Once the visitor grants analytics, the runtime activates them in document order. In the test site, matomo.example.com/matomo.js was requested only after "Accept all". You can write the same form by hand, in a view or right in a page's Markdown; the runtime treats it alike: <script type="text/plain" data-consent="analytics" data-src="https://stats.example.org/counter.js" defer></script> data-consent names the category, data-src holds the URL, and every other attribute (async, defer, integrity, …) is copied to the activated script. Note revision: 2. A visitor's stored choice carries the revision it was made under; when the built revision is higher, the banner shows again. Adding a service or a category to a site that already shows the banner does not ask returning visitors again by itself, so bump revision whenever you do. In the test site, a choice stored under revision 2 brought the banner back as soon as the site was rebuilt with revision: 3. Withdrawal in the settings dialog is stored at once but takes effect from the next page load: a script that already ran cannot be unloaded. 5. List your services on the privacy page Your privacy page should name the services you use. The plugin puts them into app.consent, per language under app.consent.locales, with the texts already resolved. Give the privacy page its own view: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main != content - const consentLocale = app.consent.locales[meta.lang || app.lang] || app.consent.locales.en each category in consentLocale.categories h2= category.label each service in category.services h3= service.name p #{service.provider}: #{service.purpose} if service.privacyUrl p a(href=service.privacyUrl rel='noopener') #{consentLocale.texts.service_privacy} if service.cookies.length table thead tr th(scope='col')= consentLocale.texts.cookie_name th(scope='col')= consentLocale.texts.cookie_duration th(scope='col')= consentLocale.texts.cookie_purpose tbody each cookie in service.cookies tr td= cookie.name td= cookie.duration td= cookie.purpose and point pages/privacy.md at it with layout: pages/privacy.pug. The table then comes from the same config as the banner and cannot drift from it: <h2>External media</h2> <h3>YouTube</h3> <p>Google Ireland Limited, Dublin: Shows embedded videos.</p> <p><a href="https://policies.google.com/privacy" rel="noopener">Privacy policy of the provider</a></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th scope="col">Name</th> <th scope="col">Duration</th> <th scope="col">Purpose</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>VISITOR_INFO1_LIVE</td> <td>6 months</td> <td>Estimates the visitor's bandwidth.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2>Statistics</h2> … The rest of the privacy policy, who you are, what your host logs, the visitor's rights, is still yours to write. 6. Theme and translate Every color and size of banner, dialog and placeholder is a --nera-consent-* custom property, so your own stylesheet can set them anywhere: :root { --nera-consent-font: system-ui, sans-serif; --nera-consent-bg: #fffbeb; --nera-consent-fg: #1c1917; --nera-consent-button-bg: #92400e; --nera-consent-button-fg: #ffffff; --nera-consent-radius: 0; } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --nera-consent-bg: #1c1917; --nera-consent-fg: #fafaf9; --nera-consent-button-bg: #fbbf24; --nera-consent-button-fg: #1c1917; } } Link it in the layout (link(rel='stylesheet' href='/css/site.css')). The plugin's README has the full table of properties. Accept all, Reject all and Settings share one set of button properties on purpose: there is no way to make one of them stand out. The defaults reach a contrast of at least 4.5:1; keep that when you change them. The texts come in English and German. Every text resolves per page language (meta.lang || app.lang), first hit wins: texts.<lang> in config/consent.yaml, then consent.<key> in your app.translations, then the built-in text. A Spanish page, for example: texts: es: banner_title: Cookies y contenido externo accept_all: Aceptar todo reject_all: Rechazar todo settings: Ajustes or, next to your other translations: translations: es: consent.placeholder_load: Cargar {service} consent.banner_text: Este sitio puede cargar contenido y servicios de terceros. Solo se cargan si das tu consentimiento. A key you do not translate falls back to English: on the Spanish test page, the banner's privacy link still read "Privacy policy". The README lists every key. A category's label and description, and a service's purpose, take one text per language the same way: - id: analytics label: en: Statistics es: Estadísticas 7. What nera build --check reports nera build --check checks the built public/ for privacy problems, among others. The output below is from @nera-static/validate 1.6.2, the version @nera-static/nera 1.17.0 brings. Later releases may report gated markup differently. Before gating, with the plain iframe in pages/video.md, no categories, and the analytics script as a plain tag in the layout's head: script(src='https://matomo.example.com/matomo.js' async) privacy-third-party reports both: public/imprint.html :24 warning loads matomo.example.com — a third-party request that sends the visitor's IP address; self-host the resource, gate the element with `data-consent` (the markup of @nera-static/plugin-consent) so it loads only after the visitor agrees, or name the host in the privacy policy and list the host under `privacy.allowed_hosts` in config/validate.yaml once it is accounted for (Art. 6 DSGVO) (on 4 pages, e.g. public/imprint.html, public/index.html, public/privacy.html, …) privacy-third-party public/video.html :30 warning loads a YouTube embed from www.youtube-nocookie.com — a third-party request that sends the visitor's IP address; consider a click-to-load placeholder (Art. 6 DSGVO, § 25 TDDDG), e.g. gate the element with `data-consent` (the markup of @nera-static/plugin-consent), or list the host under `privacy.allowed_hosts` in config/validate.yaml once it is accounted for 0 error(s), 2 warning(s) The hint "gate the element with data-consent" appears when a host's first use in a file is an element the plugin can gate: a script, iframe, embed, object, video or audio. Images, <link>s and CSS keep the plain message. After gating, with the config from steps 3 and 4 and the hand-written tag in pages/stats.md: ✓ No problems found. Validate does not read a <script> whose type is not JavaScript as a resource, and an iframe or media element with data-consent and only data-consent-* loading attributes loads nothing, so the gated markup gives no privacy-third-party finding. A tag that is marked but still loads is what privacy-consent-leak reports. Leave out type="text/plain" and keep src in the hand-written tag: <script data-consent="analytics" src="https://stats.example.org/counter.js" defer></script> and the check finds it twice: public/stats.html :33 warning loads stats.example.org — a third-party request that sends the visitor's IP address; self-host the resource, gate the element with `data-consent` (the markup of @nera-static/plugin-consent) so it loads only after the visitor agrees, or name the host in the privacy policy and list the host under `privacy.allowed_hosts` in config/validate.yaml once it is accounted for (Art. 6 DSGVO) privacy-third-party :33 warning `<script data-consent="analytics" src="https://stats.example.org/counter.js">` is marked `data-consent` but runs as JavaScript — the browser runs it before the visitor agrees; set `type="text/plain"`, rename `src` to `data-src`, as in the markup of @nera-static/plugin-consent (§ 25 TDDDG) privacy-consent-leak 0 error(s), 2 warning(s) Both are warnings, so the build still succeeds. To fail it, promote the rule in config/validate.yaml: rules: privacy-consent-leak: error privacy-consent-leak: off switches it off. The check sees only the built HTML: it cannot tell whether your privacy policy names a service, or whether a service needs consent in the first place. Defaults, not legal advice The plugin's texts and behaviour are defaults, not legal advice, and nothing here makes a site compliant with any law. What the plugin does is technical, and it holds whatever the config says: The banner and dialog name each configured service, its provider and purpose, so the consent can be informed and specific (Art. 4 Nr. 11, Art. 7 DSGVO). "Reject all" is on the first layer, as visible and as easy to use as "Accept all". Nothing is pre-selected; "necessary" is implicit and cannot be configured. Nothing gated runs or loads before consent (§ 25 (1) TDDDG). Consent can be withdrawn at any time through the settings link, without a rebuild. A revision bump asks every visitor again. Storing the visitor's choice (in localStorage, under nera-consent) is strictly necessary and needs no consent (§ 25 (2) Nr. 2 TDDDG). Whether your site needs consent, which services you list and what your banner and privacy policy say are your decisions. Check them yourself, or with someone qualified to advise you. The plugin's README and npm page have the full config reference, the markup contract and the known limitations. Next How this website is built shows the plugins of this site working together. nera.js.org itself loads nothing from another host, so it shows no banner.

title: Build a navigation with active states
description: Use plugin-navigation to render a header and footer menu, with the current page highlighted.
content: @nera-static/plugin-navigation turns a YAML list into a navigation menu and marks the link for the current page — no JavaScript required. 1. Install and publish the template npm install @nera-static/plugin-navigation npx nera-navigation The second command copies the nav templates into theme/views/vendor/plugin-navigation/, where you can edit them freely. 2. Define the menu Create config/navigation.yaml. A single flat menu looks like this: active_class: nav__link--active active_path_class: nav__link--active-path nav_class: nav elements: - href: /index.html name: Home - href: /docs/index.html name: Docs All three class keys are optional, and the values above are their defaults, so this example renders the same as one without them. active_class goes on the link to the current page, active_path_class on a section link — one pointing at a folder's index, such as /docs/index.html or /docs/ — when the current page sits in that folder or below (the site root never counts). nav_class is the BEM block name the other classes derive from: nav_class: mainmenu renames the whole family to .mainmenu, .mainmenu--list, .mainmenu__item, .mainmenu__link, .mainmenu__link--active and .mainmenu__link--active-path. The two state keys override just their own class, so when you rename, drop them — left as above, they keep nav__link--active. Every entry needs an href: one without it is skipped with a warning, and the build still succeeds. Upgrading from 2.x? Publishing skips an existing theme/views/vendor/plugin-navigation/, so the old templates stay and nav_class seems to do nothing. Run npx nera-navigation --force once — it overwrites that folder, so if you edited your copy, save your changes first and carry them over. Need more than one menu? Nest them under names — each becomes app.nav.<name>.elements: elements: main: - href: /index.html name: Home - href: /docs/index.html name: Docs footer: - href: /about.html name: About The plugin exposes everything under app.nav. 3. Render it in a layout Include the published partial and call its mixin: include /vendor/plugin-navigation/partials/link-list-navigation header.site-header if app.nav && app.nav.main nav.nav--main(aria-label='Main menu') +linkListNav(app.nav.main.elements) The plugin adds the active class from section 2 (nav__link--active by default) to the link matching the current page, and the active-path class (nav__link--active-path) to the section link the page sits in, so styling the current section is just CSS. The nav with its aria-label makes the menu a named navigation landmark for screen readers. The leading / in the include resolves from theme/views/, wherever the including file sits. Prefer a different shape? The plugin also ships simple-navigation and pipe-separated-navigation partials — same data, different markup. This site uses exactly this setup for its header and footer — see config/navigation.yaml in the source.

title: Open external links in a new tab
description: Use plugin-link-attributes to add target and rel to outbound links automatically.
content: @nera-static/plugin-link-attributes post-processes your rendered HTML and adds attributes to outbound links — so every external link opens in a new tab, safely, without you touching the Markdown. 1. Install npm install @nera-static/plugin-link-attributes No template to publish — this plugin only transforms content. Its one setting lives in a config file. 2. Configure config/link-attributes.yaml lists the attributes to add. The quick way to get it is the plugin's own command, which writes the defaults shown below: npx nera-link-attributes An existing file is left alone, so re-running never overwrites your edits; npx nera-link-attributes --force replaces it with a fresh copy. You can also write the file by hand: attributes: - target="_blank" - rel="noopener noreferrer" Without any attributes the plugin leaves your pages unchanged — no file, no new tabs. The plugin targets only links whose href starts with http or www, so your internal links (/docs/...) are left alone, and an attribute a link already has is never overwritten. The rel="noopener noreferrer" is worth keeping — it closes the tab-nabbing hole that bare target="_blank" opens. 3. The one gotcha: layout links The plugin rewrites links inside your Markdown content, not links you write directly in Pug layouts (a header "GitHub" button, a footer link). Add the same attributes to those by hand: a.site-header__cta(href=app.repo_url, target="_blank", rel="noopener noreferrer") GitHub Render, and every outbound link — in content and in your layout — opens in a new tab. This site does exactly this; try any GitHub link.

title: How this website is built
description: A case study of the Nera site itself — the plugins, the ordering, the local plugins, and how it is checked and deployed.
content: This whole site is built with Nera. Nothing here is special-cased — it's the same generator and the same public plugins you'd install. Here's the full recipe. Scaffolded like any site It started with the nera CLI, which scaffolds a site whose one Nera dependency is @nera-static/nera (it brings the @nera-static/core engine): npx @nera-static/nera new nera-website Thirteen plugins, each doing one thing Plugin Job Config plugin-navigation Header + footer menus with active states config/navigation.yaml plugin-tags Tutorial tags + per-language /tutorials/tags/* pages config/tags.yaml plugin-search Per-language client-side search index + box config/search.yaml plugin-page-pagination Prev/next in docs and tutorials config/page-pagination.yaml plugin-canonical-links Canonical <link> tags for SEO config/canonical-links.yaml plugin-link-attributes External links open in a new tab config/link-attributes.yaml plugin-code-blocks Build-time syntax highlighting with a copy button config/code-blocks.yaml plugin-stacks The homepage feature grid, one Markdown file per feature in pages/stacks/home-features/ (see Reusable content blocks) — tutorials-list (local) Builds app.tutorials for the index — llms-txt (local) llms.txt, llms-full.txt and a .md per page for AI assistants config/llms-txt.yaml skill-zip (local) The Nera skill as a zip for claude.ai and Claude Desktop — heading-ids (local) An id on every h2–h4, so sections can be linked — table-scroll (local) Wraps every Markdown table in a .table-scroll box, so wide tables scroll on phones — The five local plugins — tutorials-list, llms-txt, skill-zip, heading-ids and table-scroll — live in plugins/, set with folders.plugins in config/app.yaml. llms-txt and skill-zip write files rather than data, and hand them to the build through the getAssets hook (see Write your own local plugin). skill-zip reads the skill from the installed @nera-static/nera, so the download always matches the CLI the site builds with. Most of the others have their own tutorial in this section, if you want the details. Order matters — canonical links and search run last Search builds its index from the final state of every page, so it has to run after everything else. Canonical links have to come after plugin-tags too, or the tag pages it generates get no canonical link — and alphabetically, canonical-links would run before tags. config/plugin-order.yaml says so: plugin-order: - end: - plugin-canonical-links - plugin-search Everything else runs alphabetically in between. This is the one place plugin ordering is load-bearing on this site. Templates we own Plugins that ship views were published into theme/views/vendor/ with commands like npx nera-navigation. Those copies are ours to edit and style — nothing important is hidden inside node_modules. Content is just Markdown Every page you're reading is a Markdown file under pages/ with a layout in its frontmatter. The docs are pages/docs/*.md; this tutorial is pages/tutorials/how-this-site-is-built.md. Folders become URLs; no routing config exists. Build npm run build # pages/ -> public/ Checks and deploy Every push to main and every pull request against it runs .github/workflows/test.yml on Node 22 and 24 — the same commands you can run locally: npm ci npm run lint # eslint npm test # node --test on the tests beside the local plugins npm run validate # nera validate: layouts, includes, frontmatter npm run build -- --check # nera build --check --check looks at the built public/ for accessibility, privacy and legal-notice problems and reports what it finds. Findings are warnings, so they fail the run only for a rule that config/validate.yaml promotes to an error. A push to main then runs .github/workflows/deploy.yml: npm ci, npm run build, and public/ is published to GitHub Pages — the site you are reading at nera.js.org. That's the entire stack: Markdown in, static HTML out, plugins for the rest. If you've read the other tutorials in this section, you've now seen every piece of it in isolation — this is just all of them together.

title: Tutorials
description: Step-by-step guides for building real sites with Nera and its plugins.
content: Hands-on guides for building real things with Nera — from a first blog to wiring up individual plugins. Browse by topic below, or read the latest.

title: Build a one-page site
description: A single scrolling landing page from one Markdown file per section, with an in-page navigation, a mailto contact form and social links in the footer.
content: A freelancer or a small business often needs one page, not a site: a hero, the services, a few words about who you are, and a way to get in touch, all on one scrolling page. In this tutorial you build that page with each section in its own Markdown file. @nera-static/plugin-one-page merges the sections into the home page, @nera-static/plugin-page-navigation adds the in-page links, @nera-static/plugin-contact-form adds a contact form without a backend, and @nera-static/plugin-social-media-links puts your profiles in the footer. Want a finished business site to edit instead? The business starter sets one up with a theme, sample pages for services, about, opening hours and contact, a contact form and social links: npx @nera-static/nera new my-site --starter business Its files won't match the steps below: the starter builds a site of several pages, while this tutorial builds a single page by hand, to show how the pieces fit together. 1. Scaffold and install npx @nera-static/nera new my-site cd my-site npm install @nera-static/plugin-one-page @nera-static/plugin-page-navigation \ @nera-static/plugin-contact-form @nera-static/plugin-social-media-links Nera finds all four plugins on its own. Three of them ship templates. Publish them into your views folder, where they are yours to edit: npx nera-page-navigation npx nera-contact-form npx nera-social-media-links On a nera new site they land in theme/views/vendor/plugin-<name>/, and the contact form's client script in theme/assets/js/contact-form.js. plugin-one-page ships no template and needs no config file. 2. The target page The page the sections are merged into is an ordinary page. Here it is the home page, and its own content is the hero: --- layout: pages/one-page.pug title: Studio Lena description: Web design for small businesses in Berlin --- # Websites for small businesses I design and build fast, simple websites for shops, studios and practices. Give it a template of its own. It grows in the next steps; for now it renders the content: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main != content 3. One file per section Each section is a Markdown file that names its target page in add_to_page and its position in add_to_page_order. Keep them together in pages/sections/: --- title: Services add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 1 anchor_id: services content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--services --- ## Services - **New websites**: from the first sketch to the live site. - **Redesigns**: a fresh look for the site you already have. - **Care plans**: updates and small changes every month. --- title: About add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 2 anchor_id: about content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--about --- ## About I'm Lena, a web designer in Berlin. I have built sites for small businesses since 2015. --- title: Contact add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 3 anchor_id: contact content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--contact --- ## Contact Tell me about your project. The form opens your own email program with the message ready to send. Run npx nera build. Until step 7 it also warns that plugin-contact-form has no recipient configured; the form simply does not render yet. public/index.html now holds the hero followed by the three sections, in their order (shortened): <main id="main"> <h1>Websites for small businesses</h1> <p>I design and build fast, simple websites for shops, studios and practices.</p> <section class="section section--services"> <a id="services"></a> <h2>Services</h2> <ul> <li><strong>New websites</strong>: from the first sketch to the live site.</li> … </ul> </section> <section class="section section--about"> <a id="about"></a> <h2>About</h2> … </section> <section class="section section--contact"> <a id="contact"></a> <h2>Contact</h2> … </section> </main> The sections are always appended after the target page's own content. Each one is wrapped in a <section>; content_wrapper_tag sets another element, and content_wrapper_tag: '' drops the wrapper. The wrapper attributes are a plain mapping or a list of { attribute, value } entries, and their values are HTML-escaped. Quote a value that contains : : content_wrapper_attributes: style: 'background-color: #f5f5f5;' Unquoted, the frontmatter does not parse: the build logs ❌ Failed to process page …: Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings …, drops the page and still exits 0. nera validate reports it as a yaml-parse error. add_to_page must match exactly add_to_page is compared literally with the target page's href, which always starts with / and ends in .html: pages/index.md is /index.html, pages/de/index.md is /de/index.html. With add_to_page: index.html nothing is merged, and the build says so: ⚠️ one-page: no page has href "index.html" — 1 section(s) targeting it were not merged. `add_to_page` must match a page's href exactly, e.g. "/index.html" for pages/index.md 4. Anchors Each section gets an empty <a id="…"> in front of its content, so /index.html#services jumps to it. anchor_id sets the id. Without it, the plugin derives one from the section's first <h1>, slugified: lowercase, accents removed, everything else turned into -. This section has no anchor_id: --- title: Team add_to_page: /index.html add_to_page_order: 4 --- # Über uns Zwei Leute, ein Studio. It is merged as: <section> <a id="uber-uns"></a> <h1>Über uns</h1> <p>Zwei Leute, ein Studio.</p> </section> Lower headings are ignored, so a section with only ## headings gets no anchor unless you set anchor_id. And an <h1> per section is not what you want on a one-page site: the home page already has its <h1>, and with team.md in place nera build --check warns page has more than one <h1> (a11y-h1). So give the sections ## headings and an explicit anchor_id, as in step 3, and delete team.md again. Explicit ids also stay the same when you rename a heading or translate the page (see step 10). 5. Sections without a page of their own A section is still a page of its own. Nera writes a page only if it has a layout, and the sections above have none, so they exist only inside /index.html. Add layout: pages/default.pug to about.md and the build also writes /sections/about.html, while the section still appears on the home page. Leave layout out unless you want that second URL. nera validate does not know that the missing layout is on purpose: pages/sections/about.md warning page has no `layout` — the build skips it silently; add `layout: pages/default.pug` to its frontmatter (a template in theme/views), or, if it has none on purpose (a fragment or draft), add `ignore: { layout-missing: [pages/sections/about.md] }` to config/validate.yaml layout-missing … 0 error(s), 3 warning(s) Because all sections live in one folder, one entry silences them all: ignore: layout-missing: - pages/sections A folder covers everything below it. nera validate now prints ✓ No problems found. 6. In-page navigation plugin-page-navigation builds a navigation of sibling pages in the same folder, and skips pages at the site root, so on its own it gives index.md nothing. Its other mode fits: a page_navigation list in the page's frontmatter, whose entries go to the template exactly as written. Point them at the anchors: --- layout: pages/one-page.pug title: Studio Lena description: Web design for small businesses in Berlin page_navigation: - href: '#services' name: Services - href: '#about' name: About - href: '#contact' name: Contact --- # Websites for small businesses I design and build fast, simple websites for shops, studios and practices. Quote the hrefs: in YAML an unquoted # after a space starts a comment.
