Include the published template above the content: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main include /vendor/plugin-page-navigation/page-navigation != content The <nav> is named by the translation key Page navigation, so it stays distinct from a main menu for screen readers. Give it a label in your language in config/app.yaml: translations: en: Page navigation: On this page The built page starts with: <nav class="page-nav" aria-label="On this page"><a class="page-nav__link" href="#services">Services</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#about">About</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#contact">Contact</a></nav> You could write these three links into the template by hand just as well. The plugin earns its place once the links differ per page or per language: they live in each page's frontmatter, next to the content they point to. 7. The contact form plugin-contact-form renders a form from config/contact-form.yaml. On submit a small script in the browser builds a mailto: link from the fields and opens the visitor's own email program with subject and message filled in. There is no backend: your site stores and sends nothing, and the message leaves only through the visitor's email. (Handling the form on a server is not covered here.) recipient: hello@example.com subject: contact_subject submit_label: contact_submit error_required: contact_required error_email: contact_email_invalid fields: - { name: name, label: contact_name, type: text, required: true } - { name: email, label: contact_email, type: email, required: true } - name: topic label: contact_topic type: select required: true options: - { value: new-site, label: contact_topic_new } - { value: redesign, label: contact_topic_redesign } - { value: care, label: contact_topic_care } - { name: message, label: contact_message, type: textarea, required: true } Every user-facing value here is a translation key, resolved for each page's language from translations: in config/app.yaml. A key without a translation renders as written, so a site in one language could write the text directly; keys pay off in step 10. name and the option values are data and are never translated. Add the English texts: translations: en: Page navigation: On this page contact_subject: Enquiry from the website contact_submit: Open in my email program contact_required: Please fill in all required fields. contact_email_invalid: Please enter a valid email address. contact_name: Your name contact_email: Your email contact_topic: What can I help with? contact_topic_new: A new website contact_topic_redesign: A redesign contact_topic_care: A care plan contact_message: Your message Keep the keys nera new put under en: (app_description, skip_to_content and the others) next to these. The form is Pug, so it goes in the template, not in a Markdown section. The contact section has the highest add_to_page_order, so the form placed after the content follows its text directly: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main include /vendor/plugin-page-navigation/page-navigation != content include /vendor/plugin-contact-form/contact-form The built form (shortened): <form class="contact-form" novalidate="novalidate" data-contact-form="data-contact-form"> <script type="application/json" data-contact-config="data-contact-config"> { "subject": "Enquiry from the website", … } </script><span class="contact-form__recipient" hidden="hidden" data-contact-recipient="&#104;&#101;&#108;&#108;&#111;&#64;&#101;&#120;&#97;&#109;&#112;&#108;&#101;&#46;&#99;&#111;&#109;"></span> <div class="contact-form__field contact-form__field--text"><label class="contact-form__label" for="contact-name">Your name</label><input class="contact-form__input" type="text" id="contact-name" name="name" data-contact-field="data-contact-field" data-contact-label="Your name" required="required" /></div> … <div class="contact-form__decoy" aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute;left:-9999px;top:auto;width:1px;height:1px;overflow:hidden"><label for="contact-website">website</label><input type="text" id="contact-website" name="website" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off" /></div> <div class="contact-form__status" role="alert" aria-live="polite" data-contact-status="data-contact-status"></div><button class="contact-form__submit" type="submit">Open in my email program</button> </form> <script src="/js/contact-form.js"></script> Submitted with every field filled in, the form opened this link: mailto:hello@example.com?subject=Enquiry%20from%20the%20website&body=Your%20name%3A%20Jane%20Doe%0D%0AYour%20email%3A%20jane%40example.org%0D%0AWhat%20can%20I%20help%20with%3F%3A%20redesign%0D%0AYour%20message%3A%20Hello%20Lena Submitted empty, it opened nothing and showed Please fill in all required fields. in the status line. Three details are worth knowing: The recipient is obfuscated, not hidden. It never appears as readable text, but it is in the page: obfuscation What lands in the HTML Strength entities (default) each character as an HTML entity, as above deters naïve scrapers; a determined one can still decode it jsassembly only an array of character codes, rebuilt in JavaScript on submit stronger, still not a guarantee Use an address you are willing to publish. A honeypot is built in. The hidden website field is a decoy for bots; a submission that fills it is dropped silently. Never give a real field the honeypot's name. If you want a real "website" field, rename the decoy with honeypot: in the config. The plugin ships no CSS apart from the inline rule that hides the decoy. Style the BEM classes .contact-form, .contact-form__field, .contact-form__input and the others from your own stylesheet. 8. Social links in the footer plugin-social-media-links reads a list of links from config/social-media-links.yaml: aria_label: Social media open_in_new_tab: false social_media_links: - name: GitHub href: https://github.com/yourname icon: '<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 .297c-6.63 0-12 5.373-12 12 …"/></svg>' icon_raw: true - name: LinkedIn href: https://www.linkedin.com/in/yourname The d attribute is shortened here; paste the full path of the icon you use. Simple Icons (simpleicons.org) has brand logos as SVG. icon is escaped unless the entry sets icon_raw: true, so set it only for markup you wrote or checked yourself. The LinkedIn entry has no icon and shows its name only. The plugin's sample config uses Font Awesome <i> tags instead, which need the Font Awesome CSS. Loading it from a CDN sends every visitor's IP address to a third party, and nera build --check then warns privacy-third-party. Inline SVG or plain text needs no request at all. open_in_new_tab: false lets the visitor decide where a link opens; without it, every link gets target="_blank". rel="noopener noreferrer" is set either way. Include the published template in the footer of the base layout that nera new created. Remove its first line, the //- nera:scaffold-default marker, now that the file is your own: <!DOCTYPE html> html(lang=app.lang) head meta(charset="UTF-8") meta(name="viewport", content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0") title #{ meta.title } | #{ app.name } meta(name="description", content=`${ meta.description || t('app_description') }`) meta(name="keywords", content=`${ meta.keywords || t('app_keywords') }`) meta(name="generator" content="nera") meta(name="robots" content=`${ meta.robots || app.robots }`) style. .skip-link { position: absolute; left: -9999px; } .skip-link:focus { position: static; } body a.skip-link(href="#main") #{ t('skip_to_content') } block content footer include /vendor/plugin-social-media-links/social-media-links a(href="/imprint.html") #{ t('imprint') } = ' · ' a(href="/privacy.html") #{ t('privacy') } The footer now starts with (SVG path shortened): <footer> <nav class="social-media-links" aria-label="Social media"> <ul class="social-media-links__list"> <li class="social-media-links__item"><a class="social-media-links__link" href="https://github.com/yourname" title="GitHub" rel="noopener noreferrer"><span class="social-media-links__icon"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 .297c-6.63 0-12 5.373-12 12 …"/></svg></span><span class="social-media-links__label">GitHub</span></a></li> <li class="social-media-links__item"><a class="social-media-links__link" href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/yourname" title="LinkedIn" rel="noopener noreferrer"><span class="social-media-links__icon"></span><span class="social-media-links__label">LinkedIn</span></a></li> </ul> </nav><a href="/imprint.html">Imprint</a> · <a href="/privacy.html">Privacy</a> </footer> 9. Scrolling under a sticky navigation A little CSS makes the page feel like one: the navigation stays at the top, the links scroll smoothly, and a section does not end up hidden under the navigation. Create theme/assets/css/site.css: html { scroll-behavior: smooth; } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { html { scroll-behavior: auto; } } .page-nav { position: sticky; top: 0; display: flex; gap: 1rem; padding: 1rem 0; background: #fff; } .section > a[id] { scroll-margin-top: 4rem; } The scroll target is the anchor, not the <section>, so scroll-margin-top goes on a[id]. Load the file in the layout's head, after the meta lines: link(rel="stylesheet", href="/css/site.css") Files in theme/assets/ are served from the site root, so the file is /css/site.css. In a headless browser, on a page long enough to scroll that far, a click on each navigation link put its heading 64 px (4rem) from the top, just below the 50 px high sticky navigation. 10. A second language A German copy of the page is a second target with its own sections. Set lang: de on each file and target /de/index.html: --- layout: pages/one-page.pug lang: de title: Studio Lena description: Webdesign für kleine Unternehmen in Berlin page_navigation: - href: '#services' name: Leistungen - href: '#about' name: Über mich - href: '#contact' name: Kontakt --- # Websites für kleine Unternehmen Ich gestalte und baue schnelle, einfache Websites für Läden, Studios und Praxen. --- lang: de title: Leistungen add_to_page: /de/index.html add_to_page_order: 1 anchor_id: services content_wrapper_attributes: class: section section--services --- ## Leistungen - **Neue Websites**: von der ersten Skizze bis zur fertigen Seite. - **Redesigns**: ein frischer Auftritt für die Website, die Sie schon haben. - **Pflege**: Updates und kleine Änderungen jeden Monat. about.md and contact.md in pages/de/sections/ follow the same pattern with anchor_id: about and anchor_id: contact. The anchors stay the same in both languages, so the CSS works for both and a link to #contact works on either page. Extend the ignore entry to every language folder; * stands for one folder name: ignore: layout-missing: - pages/sections - pages/*/sections Translate the keys from steps 6 and 7 under de: in config/app.yaml: de: app_description: Eine statische Website, gebaut mit Nera app_keywords: nera, static site generator skip_to_content: Zum Inhalt springen imprint: Impressum privacy: Datenschutz Page navigation: Auf dieser Seite contact_subject: Anfrage über die Website contact_submit: In meinem E-Mail-Programm öffnen contact_required: Bitte füllen Sie alle Pflichtfelder aus. contact_email_invalid: Bitte geben Sie eine gültige E-Mail-Adresse ein. contact_name: Ihr Name contact_email: Ihre E-Mail-Adresse contact_topic: Wobei kann ich helfen? contact_topic_new: Eine neue Website contact_topic_redesign: Ein Redesign contact_topic_care: Ein Pflegepaket contact_message: Ihre Nachricht The scaffolded layout sets html(lang=app.lang), which is en on every page. Use the page's language instead: html(lang=meta.lang || app.lang) /de/index.html then has <html lang="de">, the German navigation and the German form, with the same field names: <nav class="page-nav" aria-label="Auf dieser Seite"><a class="page-nav__link" href="#services">Leistungen</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#about">Über mich</a><a class="page-nav__link" href="#contact">Kontakt</a></nav> … <div class="contact-form__field contact-form__field--text"><label class="contact-form__label" for="contact-name">Ihr Name</label><input class="contact-form__input" type="text" id="contact-name" name="name" data-contact-field="data-contact-field" data-contact-label="Ihr Name" required="required" /></div> The social links' aria_label is not passed through t() by the shipped template. To translate it, change the nav line in your published theme/views/vendor/plugin-social-media-links/social-media-links.pug: nav.social-media-links(aria-label=t(app.socialMediaLinksLabel)) and add Social media: Soziale Medien under de:. With all of this in place, nera validate and nera build --check both print ✓ No problems found. One page or stacks? plugin-stacks also turns Markdown files into pieces of other pages, but the other way round. A stack is a block that a view places, anywhere and as often as you like, through app.stacks; it marks itself with type: stack and needs no validate.yaml entry. A one-page section names its target page in add_to_page, and the plugin appends it to that page's content, in order, with an anchor and a wrapper, without touching a template. Use one-page when a page is a sequence of sections. Use stacks when the same block belongs in several places or in a particular spot of a layout. Next Build a navigation with active states adds a main menu, once the one page grows into a few. How this website is built shows a complete Nera site with its plugins working together.

title: Add prev/next links between pages
description: Use plugin-page-pagination to link sibling pages in reading order.
content: @nera-static/plugin-page-pagination links each page to its previous and next sibling — pages in the same directory — in an order you control. Perfect for docs and multi-part tutorials. 1. Install and publish the template npm install @nera-static/plugin-page-pagination npx nera-page-pagination 2. Order the pages By default the plugin reads a pagination_order number from each page: --- title: Getting started pagination_order: 2 --- Pages are ordered by pagination_order first, then by creation date, then by path — so a page without an explicit order still lands somewhere stable. Ordering starts at 0 if you want it to: the plugin treats 0 as a real value, not "missing". Change the key name in config/page-pagination.yaml with order_property if you prefer. 3. Render the links The plugin adds meta.pagePagination with .previous and .next. Include the published template, guarded so it's hidden when there's nowhere to go: if meta.pagePagination && (meta.pagePagination.previous || meta.pagePagination.next) include ../vendor/plugin-page-pagination/page-pagination Why "siblings only" matters Pagination is scoped per directory, so pages/docs/*.md paginate among themselves and pages/tutorials/*.md among themselves — they never bleed into each other. Put a sequence in its own folder and it just works. This site's docs use exactly this.

title: Reusable content blocks with plugin-stacks
description: Write sections once in Markdown and place them in any view with plugin-stacks, as single blocks or as ordered, per-language stack groups.
content: Some content belongs to no single page: a call to action under every article, a newsletter box, the feature grid on a homepage. @nera-static/plugin-stacks lets you write such a block once, as a Markdown file in pages/, and place it in any view through app.stacks. Several blocks that form one section become a stack group, ordered and split by language. 1. Install npm install @nera-static/plugin-stacks Nera finds the plugin on its own. It needs no config file: stacks are defined in frontmatter. 2. What makes a page a stack A stack is a Markdown file under pages/ whose frontmatter sets type: stack and a slug or a title. Where the file lives does not matter. A pages/stacks/ folder simply keeps the blocks together: --- type: stack title: Newsletter signup --- Get **one email a month** with what changed. Note what is missing: layout. Nera writes a page to public/ only if its frontmatter has a layout, so a stack without one stays a fragment that other pages embed, not a page of its own. nera validate and nera build --check know this: since @nera-static/validate 1.6.1 they no longer warn layout-missing for a page with type: stack. 3. Use a single stack Every stack lands in app.stacks, keyed by its slug, with the same { content, meta } shape as a page: content is the rendered HTML, meta the whole frontmatter. Without an explicit slug, the key is the title lowercased, with spaces replaced by underscores: Newsletter signup becomes newsletter_signup. Place it in a view, guarded so a missing stack does not break the page: extends ../layouts/layout block content main#main != content if app.stacks.newsletter_signup aside.newsletter!= app.stacks.newsletter_signup.content The aside then holds <p>Get <strong>one email a month</strong> with what changed.</p>. Only spaces are replaced: a title with punctuation produces a key that dot access cannot read. Set an explicit slug for such titles, or whenever you want a key that does not change when the title does. Slugs are one namespace for the whole site; if two stacks end up with the same one, the later one wins and the plugin warns. 4. Render a stack through a template A stack can bring its own markup. Publish the plugin's default template: npx nera-stacks It lands in theme/views/vendor/plugin-stacks/stack-template.pug. Point a stack at it with stack_layout, a path from the project root (where you run nera build), not from the views folder: --- type: stack slug: call_to_action title: Ready to start? description: One command scaffolds a site. stack_layout: theme/views/vendor/plugin-stacks/stack-template.pug --- Run `npx @nera-static/nera new my-site` and you are live in minutes. app.stacks.call_to_action.content now holds the template's output, not the bare Markdown: <section class="stack"> <header class="stack__header"> <h2 class="stack__title">Ready to start?</h2> <p class="stack__description">One command scaffolds a site.</p> </header> <article class="stack__content"> <p>Run <code>npx @nera-static/nera new my-site</code> and you are live in minutes.</p> </article> </section> The template reads the stack as stack.meta and stack.content, so you can edit your copy or write your own. The BEM classes are the plugin's public contract: style them from your CSS. Publishing skips a folder that already exists, so after a plugin update npx nera-stacks --force fetches the new template and overwrites your edits. 5. Stack groups A feature grid is a list of blocks. Give each block its own stack page, put them into the same stack_group, and set their order with stack_order: --- type: stack stack_group: home_features stack_order: 1 lang: en title: Markdown in, HTML out --- Author content in Markdown with YAML frontmatter. The plugin then adds two keys: app.stackGroups[<group>] — every stack of the group, in order. app.stackGroupsByLang[<group>][<lang>] — the same, split by lang. A stack without lang counts as the site's app.lang. Each entry is { content, meta } again, so a view loops over it: - const features = app.stackGroupsByLang?.home_features?.[meta.lang || app.lang] || [] each feature in features .feature h2.feature__title #{ feature.meta.title } .feature__body!= feature.content On a single-language site, each feature in app.stackGroups.home_features || [] is enough. Stacks with a numeric stack_order come first, ascending; the rest follow in build order. A grouped stack needs neither a slug nor a title, and it stays out of app.stacks unless it sets an explicit slug. In a test site with three grouped stacks, of which only one had a slug: feature_plugins, app.stacks held exactly that one next to the two ungrouped stacks: call_to_action, feature_plugins, newsletter_signup. That keeps the same section in three languages from colliding on title-derived keys. 6. A real example: this site's feature grid The four boxes on the nera.js.org homepage are a stack group. Each box is one file in pages/stacks/home-features/, with translations in pages/de/stacks/home-features/ and pages/es/stacks/home-features/: --- type: stack stack_group: home_features stack_order: 1 lang: en title: Markdown in, HTML out --- Author content in Markdown with YAML frontmatter. Nera renders each page through a Pug layout you control and writes plain, fast HTML. The homepage view picks the boxes for the current language and numbers them from their position in the list: - const features = app.stackGroupsByLang?.home_features?.[curLang] || [] if features.length .home-body__grid each feature, i in features .home-body__feature p.home-body__feature-num #{ String(i + 1).padStart(2, '0') } h2.home-body__feature-title #{ feature.meta.title } .home-body__feature-desc!= feature.content curLang is set in the site's base layout from meta.lang. Adding a fifth box is one new Markdown file per language, with no change to the view. 7. Pitfall: stack pages are still pages A stack has no layout, so it is never built, but it stays in the page list every other plugin sees. In a test site with stacks in pages/stacks/, the plugins behaved like this: plugin sees stack pages? what to do plugin-search no — pages without layout are left out of the index nothing plugin-page-pagination no — a page without layout is never a previous/next target nothing plugin-navigation no — it lists only the hrefs in config/navigation.yaml nothing plugin-statistics yes — it counts every Markdown file under pages/ keep the counted keys (tags, category, …) off stack pages plugin-simple-page-list yes — with page_path: /stacks, it listed every stack with an href like /stacks/newsletter.html that was never built keep stacks out of listed folders, or exclude them with exclude_pages The exclude_pages entries use the stack's would-be page URL: page_path: /blog exclude_pages: - /blog/newsletter.html A folder of its own, like pages/stacks/, is the simpler fix: no listed path matches it, so nothing needs excluding. Next How this website is built shows how plugin-stacks works together with the other plugins on this site. To merge whole sections into one scrolling page instead, see Build a one-page site.

title: Tag your content and get topic pages for free
description: Add tags to pages with plugin-tags and get auto-generated tag overview pages and a tag cloud.
content: @nera-static/plugin-tags reads a tags: field from your frontmatter, then builds a browsable overview page for every tag automatically. 1. Install and publish templates npm install @nera-static/plugin-tags npx nera-tags 2. Tag some pages Add a comma-separated tags value to any page's frontmatter: --- layout: pages/tutorial.pug title: Add client-side search tags: plugins, search --- Tags are slugified and case-folded, so Web Dev, web dev and WEB DEV all map to one page at /tags/web-dev.html. 3. Configure (optional) config/tags.yaml — every key is optional: meta_property_name: tags tag_overview_path: '/tags' tag_separator: ',' tag_overview_layout: pages/tag-overview.pug The tag_overview_layout points at a layout that renders the published overview template. Create theme/views/pages/tag-overview.pug: extends ../layouts/layout block content .container include ../vendor/plugin-tags/pages/tag-overview 4. Show tags on a page The plugin gives each page a meta.tagLinks list. Include the published partial in your article layout: if meta.tagLinks include ../vendor/plugin-tags/partials/tag-links And for a site-wide cloud, app.tagCloud drives the tag-cloud partial: if app.tagCloud include ../vendor/plugin-tags/partials/tag-cloud 5. Per-language tags (optional) By default every tag lives in one namespace, so a multilingual site merges all languages into one overview page. Set group_by_lang to give each language its own: group_by_lang: true Tags are then collected per meta.lang, and the language code prefixes the whole tag_overview_path. With tag_overview_path: '/tutorials/tags' you get: /tutorials/tags/<slug>.html # default language /de/tutorials/tags/<slug>.html # German pages only /es/tutorials/tags/<slug>.html # Spanish pages only The default language stays unprefixed, which is what you want when it is served from the root. If every language sits in its own directory, add prefix_default_lang: true so it gets a segment too. Pages without a meta.lang fall into the default language rather than a bucket of their own, so a single-language site is unaffected by any of this. Chips and clouds follow along on their own: meta.tagLinks links within the page's own language, and each page gets a meta.tagCloud scoped to it. Watch one detail — app.tagCloud still exists, but with grouping on it holds the default language's cloud. Guarding on it is fine; reading it directly to render a cloud is not, because a German page would show English tags. The shipped tag-cloud partial already prefers meta.tagCloud and falls back to app.tagCloud, so use the partial rather than looping yourself. app.tagCloudByLang has every language, keyed by code, if you need them all at once. Generated overview pages also carry their own meta.lang, so t() inside the overview layout resolves in that page's language. Render, and every tag now has its own page — no manual index maintenance. The tutorial you're reading is tagged this way; the chips above link to the generated tag pages. This site runs with group_by_lang: true, so those chips lead to the tag pages for whichever language you are reading.

title: Write your own local plugin
description: Build a project-local plugin that adds data to app with the getAppData hook and writes a file into public/ with the getAssets hook.
content: You don't need to publish to npm to extend Nera. Any module at src/plugins/<name>/index.js is discovered and applied automatically — that is the default, and a site made with nera new has no setting for it. To keep local plugins elsewhere, set folders.plugins in config/app.yaml — this site uses plugins/: folders: plugins: ./plugins Let's build a real one: a plugin that collects every tutorial into a list for an index page — a simplified version of the plugin that powers this site — and then publishes the same list as tutorials.json. The contract A plugin exports any of three hooks: export function getAppData({ app, pagesData }) { // must return a plain object — becomes the new `app` } export function getMetaData({ app, pagesData }) { // must return an array — becomes the new `pagesData` } export function getAssets({ app, pagesData }) { // must return an array of { from, to } — files core copies into public/ } getAppData runs first; getMetaData sees the app it returned. getAssets (core ≥ 4.13.0) runs once every plugin is done with the other two. Nera awaits all hooks (since core 4.3.0; older versions silently replaced app with a Promise), but synchronous stays the safe default — it is what the published plugins do. A hook that returns the wrong type does not stop the build: core prints a warning such as ⚠️ Plugin "tutorials-list" getAppData returned invalid format, skipping replace. and keeps the old data. When a plugin seems to do nothing, read the build log first. "The hook contract" in the plugin docs has the short version. Build it Create src/plugins/tutorials-list/index.js: export function getAppData({ app, pagesData }) { if (!app || typeof app !== 'object') return app if (!Array.isArray(pagesData)) return app const tutorials = pagesData .filter(({ meta }) => { const href = meta?.href || '' return href.startsWith('/tutorials/') && href !== '/tutorials/index.html' }) .map(({ meta }) => ({ href: meta.href, title: meta.title || meta.href, description: meta.description || '', createdAt: meta.createdAt, })) .sort((a, b) => { const da = new Date(a.createdAt).getTime() const db = new Date(b.createdAt).getTime() if (!Number.isNaN(da) && !Number.isNaN(db) && da !== db) return db - da return String(a.href).localeCompare(String(b.href)) }) return { ...app, tutorials } } That's the whole plugin. It reads every page, keeps the ones under /tutorials/, and returns a new app with a sorted tutorials array. Use it in a layout app.tutorials is now available in every view: if app.tutorials && app.tutorials.length ul.tutorials__list each post in app.tutorials li.tutorials__item a.tutorials__link(href=post.href) h2 #{ post.title } p #{ post.description } Hand over a file with getAssets Now publish the same list as /tutorials.json. Writing it into public/ from a hook does not work: plugins run before core deletes and re-creates public/, so the file is gone by the end of the build. Write it into .nera-cache/tutorials-list/ instead (nera new puts .nera-cache in .gitignore) and return it from getAssets. Add this to the same file: import fs from 'fs' import path from 'path' // getAppData from above stays as it is export function getAssets({ app }) { if (!Array.isArray(app?.tutorials)) return [] const dir = path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.nera-cache/tutorials-list') const from = path.join(dir, 'tutorials.json') fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true }) fs.writeFileSync(from, `${JSON.stringify(app.tutorials, null, 4)}\n`) return [{ from, to: 'tutorials.json' }] } Each entry is { from, to }: from is an absolute path to a file or folder, to a path relative to public/ — the target file for a file, the folder its contents go into for a folder ('' is public/ itself). getAssets sees the final app, so app.tutorials from your own getAppData is already there. After nera build, public/tutorials.json holds the list, newest first: [ { "href": "/tutorials/second.html", "title": "Second tutorial", "description": "The newer one.", "createdAt": "2026-08-01T00:00:00.000Z" }, { "href": "/tutorials/first.html", "title": "First tutorial", "description": "The older one.", "createdAt": "2026-07-01T00:00:00.000Z" } ] Core copies the files in the order theme → plugins → site, so a file of the same name in your own theme/assets/ still wins. The copy happens before base_path and asset hashing, so both cover plugin files too. An entry with a relative from or a to outside public/ is skipped with a warning, such as ⚠️ Plugin "tutorials-list" getAssets entry skipped: "from" must be an absolute path (…). For real-world examples, see this site's llms-txt and skill-zip plugins. Why return a new object Nera threads each hook's return value into the next. Returning { ...app, tutorials } (rather than mutating app) keeps that data flow predictable — the same reason the built-in plugins do it. From here, the same pattern builds related-posts lists, author pages, "recently updated" widgets — anything derived from your content.
